title: The sick first (ch. 36)
hookLine: care of the sick is placed above all

lines: BEFORE ALL THINGS, ABOVE ALL THINGS.
cards: Before all things, and above all things. Strong words for any rule to use, and Saint Benedict doesn't spend them lightly. Earlier this week the Rule said nothing is to be put before the work of God.
So what could come before all things? Not the abbot. Not the chapel.
Not the harvest or the library. Chapter thirty-six answers in its first line, and the answer is the brother lying in the infirmary with a fever.

teach.h: THE SICK: BEFORE ALL, ABOVE ALL.
teach.b: Benedict writes that care of the sick must come before all things and above all things, so that they are served as Christ himself.
He gives Christ's words from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "sick, and you visited me," and "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."
One way to hold the two "before" lines together: the work of God comes first, and the sick are served as Christ. The same Christ, in the chapel and in the sickbed. Then Benedict gets specific.

teach.h: A ROOM, A CAREFUL NURSE, BATHS, MEAT.
teach.b: The sick get their own room, and a brother to look after them who is God-fearing, careful and attentive. They may have baths as often as it helps them.
The very weak may eat meat, normally kept off the monks' table, to get their strength back; when they recover, they go back to the usual fare.

The abbot takes the greatest care that the sick suffer no neglect, and checks that the cellarer and attendants let nothing slip. Here's the part that keeps it honest. Benedict speaks to the sick, too.
They should remember they're served for the honor of God, and not wear out their brothers with unreasonable demands.
Then, in the very next breath, he tells the brothers: bear with them patiently anyway, because from such as these a greater reward is gained.

teach.h: PATIENCE ON BOTH SIDES OF THE BED.
teach.b: Patience is asked of both sides of the bed.
Nobody in this chapter is a saint already. They're just people being asked to carry each other.

how: Benedictine communities care for their sick and elderly members within the monastery, and Catholics count visiting the sick among the corporal works of mercy drawn from Matthew 25.

o: letting the sick skip prayers, but nothing else
sending sick monks home until they recover
caring for the sick before all other things

p: before all things, above all things

s: in the Rule, the sick are left to manage on their own
they get their own room and a careful attendant, and the abbot must see they suffer no neglect.
Benedict asks the sick not to wear out their brothers with unreasonable demands
and in the next breath he asks the brothers to bear with them patiently anyway.
the sick may eat meat, and keep eating it after they recover
the very weak may eat meat to regain strength; once well, they return to the usual fare.

games.q: you're nursing a sick brother who keeps asking for more than seems reasonable. what does chapter thirty-six ask of you?
o: tell him firmly that he's asking too much.
bear with him patiently: from such as these a greater reward is gained.
ask the abbot to move him somewhere else.
games.why: Benedict asks the sick not to make excessive demands, and still asks the brothers to bear with them patiently.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is sick right now, in the hospital, at home with a long illness, or worn down by something nobody sees, and hold their face in your mind for a few breaths, along with one small kindness that might reach them: a visit, a call, a meal left at the door.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, keep them in mind a little longer, kindly.

wordCard.voice: The sick first. In Benedict's Rule, care of the sick comes before all things and above all things, because they are served as Christ. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from the first line of chapter thirty-six: before all things and above all things.

carryVoice: Your line: before all things. In the chapel and at the sickbed, the same Christ is served. I'll be here tomorrow.
